newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: ABC NewsLink
More legal action in store for Telstra
The legal battle between Telstra and service providers is hotting
up, with a multi-million-dollar damages claim being prepared by
A-A-P-T.
As Australia's largest service provider, A-A-P-T, is expected to
formally lodge court papers on Friday for a $300 million damages
claim against Telstra.
At the centre of the dispute is the performance of Telstra's
billing system, which is used by A-A-P-T.
Telstra has already been in the Federal Court this year with the
Tasmanian-based service provider Q-A-I, which is seeking up to $14 million damages.
ABC NewsLink
KENNETT "TRIED TO DESTROY NCA"
A witness at the inquiry into the role of the National Crime Authority says Victorian Premier, Jeff Kennett, has been "more than scathing" of the authority.
Former Federal Parliamentarian, Peter Cleeland, accused Mr Kennett of trying to destroy the NCA.
Mr Cleeland said Mr Kennett is a dominant Premier who always put his views strongly in public.
He said Mr Kennett was highly critical of the NCA's operations in relation to investigations of John Elliott, and at least one other prominent Victorian Liberal Party identity.
DEMOCRATS TO PRESS-ON WITH CALLS FOR BABY EXPERIMENT PROBE
The Australian Democrats say they will step-up the campaign for a Royal Commission into the Commonwealth Serum Laboratories in Melbourne.
The Democrats want an inquiry into the CSL's role in medical experiments done on orphaned babies in Melbourne after World War Two, and into tests of other biological products produced by the labs.
The Federal Government says it is a matter for the Victorian Government, but Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett has ruled out a Royal Commission.
Democrats Senator, Meg Lees, says the CSL was an arm of the Federal Health Department at the time, and it is clearly a Federal duty to investigate its operations.
She says she has had countless phone calls in the past 24-hours, raising questions about other experiments and CSL products, affecting more people in other states.
DOWNER: JAPAN A MARKET WORTH PERSEVERING WITH
Foreign Affairs Minister, Alexander Downer, says jobs will be lost if Australia telegraphs racist sentiments to Asia.
Mr Downer says such sentiments would also reflect poorly on Australia morally.
He has also warned Australian companies they will make an expensive mistake if they ignore Japanese markets.
A report by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade says many Australian businesses think Japan's markets are too hard to penetrate.
CHILDCARE "SHOULD BE AN ISSUE FOR EVERYONE"
The Prime Minister's advisor on women's affairs says there must be a change in the debate on childcare, because it is not just a women's issue.
Pru Goward, who heads the Office of the Status of Women, says childcare is everyone's responsibility.
Ms Goward told a Sydney conference on work and family that over 40 percent of working men and women have dependent children.

She says the numbers are even higher in two-parent families, where 65 percent of women, and 95 percent of men work. Ms Goward says changing attitudes will be an uphill battle until childcare is seen to affect everyone, and everyone wants to have a say in its future.
FIGURES SHOW MIGRANTS MORE LIKELY TO BE UNEMPLOYED
New figures show migrants continue to have a higher unemployment rate than other Australians.
The Bureau of Statistics says last November, 9.7 percent of migrants who had arrived in Australia as adults since 1970, were unemployed.
That compares with 7.7 percent for people born in Australia, and 9.2 percent for all migrants.
The Bureau says 27 percent of all Australians were born outside the country, whereas migrants who arrived as adults after 1970 make up 10 percent of the civilian population.
Seventy-one percent of migrants who were employed in November had a job before they migrated, but less than half have remained in the same occupation.
Forty-nine percent of migrants had post-school qualifications when they arrived in Australia.
OPTUS DEFEATED IN FEDERAL COURT FIGHT WITH TELSTRA
Claims by Optus that seven so-called flexi-plans run by telecommunications rival, Telstra, are discriminatory have been thrown out by the Federal Court.
Optus argued the plans were not legitimate charging options under the Telecommunications Act, because they were not within the reach of all customers.
An STD weeknight saver flexi-plan, a family and friends flexi-plan and a business saver are among the charging options, which each have a monthly fee, and usage level requirements.
The court disagreed with Optus' argument that not everyone who joined a plan would use the service enough to reach the break-even point, and so would suffer an economic loss in joining the scheme.
Justice Mansfield said considering the very modest nature of the monthly fees and of the relevant usage thresholds, there was no real obstacle to participating in the flexi-plans.
